tuesday_carousel.caption:
Most service recovery fails because the company answers the wrong question.

The customer is not only asking, "Did you fix it?"

They are asking three questions at the same time.

Was the outcome fair?
Was the process fair?
Was I treated with respect while the issue was handled?

Service recovery research has been clear on this for decades. Tax, Brown and Chandrashekaran showed that customers judge complaint handling through multiple forms of justice: distributive, procedural and interactional.

That distinction matters.

A refund can still feel unfair if the customer had to chase five times.

An apology can still fail if the process feels slow, defensive or unclear.

A policy can be technically correct and still damage trust if the customer feels dismissed.

This is why I do not like recovery audits that only ask whether a complaint was closed. Closure is an internal status. Fairness is the customer experience.

At GWR, my team looks at the full recovery path: ownership, timing, explanation, tone, evidence and final outcome. That is how a complaint log becomes a diagnostic tool.

Service recovery is not finished when the case is closed.

It is finished when the customer can say the outcome, process and treatment were fair.

Which part of your recovery journey fails most often: outcome, process or respect?

thursday_post.topic: Field File: The closed complaint that still felt unresolved
thursday_post.caption:
Field File: the closed complaint that still felt unresolved.

A customer reported a simple service issue.

The team apologized. A small adjustment was offered. The case was marked closed.

On paper, the recovery was complete.

In the customer's words, it was not.

Why?

Because nobody explained why the issue happened. Nobody confirmed what would change. Nobody owned the next step.

The outcome was acceptable, but the process did not feel fair.

That is a common recovery blind spot. Operations often closes the visible case while leaving the emotional case open.

In mystery shopping, we separate those signals. Was there ownership? Was the explanation clear? Was the timing reasonable? Did the customer feel respected, or merely processed?

Those details decide whether recovery rebuilds confidence or simply ends the conversation.

Where are your complaint reports showing "closed" while customers still feel unconvinced?
